title: Exercise and mood
text: There is a lot of [evidences|evidence|'Evidence' is uncountable. It has no plural.] that exercise improves mood. A study in 2019 [find|found|Reporting a past study: use the past simple, 'found'.] that people who exercised felt happier. Although the study was small, [but it|it|Do not use 'although' and 'but' together.] suggests a clear link. Exercise may also [reduces|reduce|After 'may', use the base verb.] stress.

title: Growing cities
text: The number of people living in cities [have|has|The subject is 'the number', which is singular.] grown rapidly since 1950. This has a big effect [to|on|We say 'an effect on' something.] the environment. Cities produce more waste, [who|which|Use 'which' for things and 'who' for people.] can pollute rivers. As a result, many governments [has|have|'Governments' is plural, so use 'have'.] introduced recycling laws.

title: Solar power
text: Solar power [is clean|is a clean|A singular countable noun needs 'a'.] energy source. In addition, it is becoming [more cheaper|cheaper|Don't use 'more' with an -er adjective.]. However, it is less [effect|effective|You need an adjective here: effective.] in winter. Last year, solar panels [was installed|were installed|'Panels' is plural, so use 'were'.] on many homes.

title: Analysing an opening
text: The writer [portray|portrays|'The writer' is singular, so the verb needs -s.] the village as quiet and isolated. The short sentences [conveys|convey|'Sentences' is plural, so there is no -s.] a sense of tension, and the repeated image of the locked gate [suggest|suggests|The subject is 'the repeated image', which is singular, so add -s.] that strangers are not welcome. We can infer [to|from|We infer something from evidence.] the narrator's hesitation that he is afraid.

title: Two characters
text: Both characters are [anxiety|anxious|After 'are', use an adjective, not a noun.] about the future, but the writer contrasts their reactions. Maria [explain|explains|'Maria' is singular, so add -s in the present simple.] her fears openly, whereas her brother hides them. This contrast is [significance|significant|After 'is', use the adjective 'significant'.] because it reveals two different attitudes [for|towards|We say an attitude towards something.] change.

title: Evaluating an argument
text: The writer argues that school uniform [should abolished|should be abolished|This is passive: should + be + past participle.]. Her most convincing evidence [are|is|'Evidence' is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb.] a survey of 500 students. However, she does not explain why the results are [relevance|relevant|You need the adjective 'relevant'.] to all schools, so her argument is less [persuade|persuasive|After 'less', you need the adjective 'persuasive'.] than it first appears.

title: A sarcastic narrator
text: The narrator's tone is [sarcasm|sarcastic|After 'is', use the adjective 'sarcastic'.] when he describes the new headteacher. The phrase 'another brilliant idea' [imply|implies|'The phrase' is singular, so add -s.] that he does not respect her. His negative attitude becomes more [explicitly|explicit|After 'becomes', use an adjective, not an adverb.] in the final paragraph, where he openly [criticise|criticises|'He' needs -s in the present simple.] her decisions.

title: A child's perspective
text: The story is told [in|from|We say from someone's perspective.] the perspective of a ten-year-old girl. Because she does not fully understand the adult world, many important details [is|are|'Details' is plural, so use 'are'.] only implicit. The reader has to [inferring|infer|After 'has to', use the base form of the verb.] what has happened, which makes the ending more [powerfully|powerful|After 'make something more', use an adjective.].

title: Justifying an interpretation
text: In my opinion, the father is [portray|portrayed|This is passive: is + past participle 'portrayed'.] as caring but strict. To justify this view, I would point to the moment when he [refuse|refuses|'He' needs -s in the present simple.] to let his daughter go out. Later he apologises, which [show|shows|'Which' refers to the whole action, so use the singular 'shows'.] that he regrets his [harshly|harsh|Before a noun ('words'), use an adjective.] words.

title: Explicit and implicit
text: The warning on the gate is [explicitly|explicit|After 'is', use an adjective.]: 'Keep out.' However, there is also [a implicit|an implicit|Use 'an' before a vowel sound.] message in the way the house is described. The broken windows and the empty garden [suggests|suggest|The subject ('the windows and the garden') is plural, so there is no -s.] that something terrible has happened there, which creates a feeling of [tense|tension|After 'a feeling of', use a noun.].

title: Comparing two poems
text: Both poems [explores|explore|'Both poems' is plural, so there is no -s.] the theme of loss, but they convey it in different ways. The first poet uses [an|a|Use 'a' before a consonant sound: 'a gentle'.] gentle, reflective tone, whereas the second is angrier. In my view, the second poem is more [effectively|effective|After 'is more', use an adjective.] because its [emphasise|emphasis|After 'its', you need the noun 'emphasis'.] on anger feels honest.
